notes.text: favour — A good report among men, especially good men, and that hearty kindness which attends it.

Meet — They live together, and need one another. The maker - Not only as they are men, but as they are poor or rich, which difference comes from God's providence. They have one common creator, and Lord, and judge, and the one cannot despise nor grudge at the other without reflecting upon God.

glossa.text:
*It is better.* For if a man should gain the whole world, he would deservedly despise it all, that his name might be written in the heavens, and his memory be fixed eternal among the saints and the angels.

*A good name.* Which is praised by the testimony of the faithful, not of the unskilled crowd, whence: *If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ!*

*Good favour.* Because a man is praised by the good for good works: nay rather, for the gifts of merits conferred upon him is glorified the Father who is in the heavens.
*The rich and the poor.* Neither honour the rich man for his riches, nor despise the poor man for his want: because they are a divine work, and made to the image and to the work of God.

notes.text: The rod — Their power and authority. Not rest - Not continue long. The lot - Upon the habitations and persons of good men. Lest - Lest they should be driven to indirect courses to relieve themselves.

Lead them — Unto sinful courses. Israel - Upon the true Israel of God. This psalm was probably composed by Ezra, at the return of Israel from Babylon. Those who are returned, are called upon to be thankful; those who still remain there, are prayed for and encouraged, ver. 1-6. A song of degrees.

glossa.text: *A canticle.* ((CASS.)) The sixth degree: the confidence of the most faithful Christian, which he has in the Lord, is compared to the most solid mountains, that he may not be jealous of those who are happy in this world. *They that trust.* ((AUG.)) This psalm teaches, etc., *as far as* who are these? what manner of Jerusalem is that? he briefly describes it.

*The mountains round about,* that is, the angels, the prophets, the apostles are its wall: whence Isaias: *And there shall be in it a wall and a bulwark ((Isa. XXVI))*; but lest thou remain among the mountains, he adds, and the Lord round about. *Let there not then be hope in the mountains,* but in the top of the mountains: whence Isaias: *In the last days there shall be a mountain on the top ((Isa. XXI))*, etc. *They that trust.* ((CASS.)) First he affirms, etc., *as far as* because they are both many and are one. *Mount Sion.* ((HIER.)) Christ, on whom the Church is founded: that mountain, according to the letter, shall be shaken at the end of the world.

*The rod of sinners.* ((AUG.)) For they bear rule sometimes for the discipline of the good, but this shall not be always, as the prophet here plainly says: and therefore the just do not fail, because they know the time to come, in which Christ, appearing in his brightness, shall gather before him all nations, and shall divide them as a shepherd divides the kids from the sheep, and shall set the sheep on the right hand, the kids on the left. *The lot.* ((CASS.)) That is, the just chosen by lot, or who are the lot and the inheritance of God.
*Do good, O Lord.* ((ID.)) The second part, where, the people being confirmed, he prays for what he knows shall come to pass, that prosperity may come to the good, vengeance to the wicked.

*But such as turn aside.* ((ID.)) By a like sentence also do they perish who turn aside from the commands of the prince, and they who strive to will evil works; those failing, together with those who compel them to fail. *Peace upon Israel.* ((AUG.)) By one name is called the paternal inheritance, which is Christ. For he is our peace, who has made both one, who shall give us peace above peace.

notes.text: My brethren -- the equality of Christians, intimated by this name, is the ground of the admonition. Hold not the faith of our common Lord, the Lord of glory — Of which glory all who believe in him partake. With respect of persons - That is, honour none merely for being rich; despise none merely for being poor.
With gold rings — Which were not then so common as now.
Ye look upon him — With respect.

Ye distinguish not — To which the most respect is due, to the poor or to the rich. But are become evil-reasoning Judges - You reason ill, and so judge wrong: for fine apparel is no proof of worth in him that wears it.

Hearken — As if he had said, Stay, consider, ye that judge thus. Does not the presumption lie rather in favour of the poor man? Hath not God chosen the poor - That is, are not they whom God hath chosen, generally speaking, poor in this world? who yet are rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom - Consequently, the most honourable of men: and those whom God so highly honours, ought not ye to honour likewise?
Do not the rich often oppress you — By open violence; often drag you - Under colour of law.
Do not they blaspheme that worthy name — Of God and of Christ. The apostle speaks chiefly of rich heathens: but are Christians, so called, a whit behind them?
If ye fulfil the royal law — The supreme law of the great King which is love; and that to every man, poor as well as rich, ye do well. Lev. xix, 18.
Being convicted — By that very law. Exod. xxiii, 3.
Whosoever keepeth the whole law, except in one point, he is guilty of all — Is as liable to condemnation as if he had offended in every point.

glossa.text: *Do not hold the faith in respect of persons. As if he should say:* The Lord does not invite the rich to the faith and despise the poor, but he chose the poor in this world, and endowed them with faith. The world casts out the poor man, courts the rich; the faith of Christ on the contrary teaches that all the glory of the rich is as the flower of the grass, while mercy toward the poor flowers unto eternity. *Of the Lord of glory.* He names him the Lord of glory, that his commands may be obeyed, who repays with everlasting glory that which is given to the poor for love of him.

*Hearken. ((BED.))* Attend more diligently, because not those who are richer in the world, etc., *as far as* yet these he has rendered illustrious and noble by the expectation of the kingdom to come.

*Hath not God. ((BED.))* God chose the poor, who elsewhere says: *Fear not, little flock, for it hath pleased your Father to give you a kingdom.* He chose poor parents also, by whose office he himself should be nourished.

*Do not the rich.* More openly he shows whom he had called rich above, namely those who prefer riches to Christ, and, themselves strangers to the faith, oppress by power those who believe, and drag them to the judgment-seats of the more powerful. And there is another cause why they are not to be chosen, because they bring evils upon the faithful.
*They blaspheme.* In the times of the apostles many of the Gentiles and of the Jews, and especially the richer, are found to have done these things.

*If yet the law.* Because he had spoken harshly and concerning contempt of the rich, and in a manner contrary to the divine law, which commands that all be loved, lest the rich be thought to be despised altogether, he adds: as if he should say, for the aforesaid causes they are not to be chosen, but if you fulfil this law which says: *Thou shalt love thy neighbour ((Matth. XXII))*, you do well; because, although the rich are not to be chosen on account of their riches, yet they are not the less to be loved for God's sake.

*Royal.* That is, excellent, or because it is common to all, and embraces all. Or that which says: *Thou shalt not confound the person of the poor, nor honour the countenance of the mighty ((Levit. XIX))* , and elsewhere: *There shall be no difference of persons: you shall hear the little as the great, because it is the judgment of God ((Deut. I))*.

*But whosoever.* Lest they should think it a contemptible sin to transgress the law in this one matter, he adds: *But whosoever,* etc. *But offend in one, he is become guilty of all.* Truly he who offends in one point is a transgressor of the whole law, because he who sins acts against the author of the law, whom he slights in his own law, and against charity, which is the cause and mother of the whole law. Let us see this sentence from a like case: If anyone should offend me, he would offend all my brothers and friends in me, and in a manner would sin against all. So he who neglects one commandment renders useless to himself the rest, which, when fulfilled, seemed to help.

notes.text: Matt. xv, 21.
The woman was a Greek (that is, a Gentile, not a Jew) a Syrophenician or Canaanite. Canaan was also called Syrophenicia, as lying between Syria, properly so called, and Phenicia.
Matt. xv, 29.

He put his fingers into his ears — Perhaps intending to teach us, that we are not to prescribe to him (as they who brought this man attempted to do) but to expect his blessing by whatsoever means he pleases: even though there should be no proportion or resemblance between the means used, and the benefit to be conveyed thereby.

Ephphatha — This was a word of SOVEREIGN AUTHORITY, not an address to God for power to heal: such an address was needless; for Christ had a perpetual fund of power residing in himself, to work all miracles whenever he pleased, even to the raising the dead, John v, 21, 26.
Them — The blind man and those that brought him.

glossa.text: *And rising up from thence.* Leaving the Scribes and Pharisees, those calumniators, he withdrew into the parts of Tyre and Sidon, that he might heal the Tyrians and the Sidonians. *No man.* ((BEDA.)) Although he could not be hid, yet what he willed was not done. But an example, etc., *as far as* that he might free the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman from the demon, and by the faith of a Gentile woman convict the perfidy of the Scribes and the Pharisees.

*For a woman.* Mark says that the Lord was in the house when the woman came to him. Matthew says that *she crieth after us ((Matth. XV))*. By which he hints that she poured out her prayers behind him as he walked. The woman therefore came to him into the house, but because Matthew says: *He answered her not a word,* he gave it to be understood that both were silent, and that they entered in silence. And so the rest is woven together, and in nothing do they disagree.

((HIER.)) The woman is our Roman mother of the Church. The daughter is the demon-possessed barbarism of the West, whose faith made a sheep out of a dog. She seeks the crumbs of understanding; she does not desire the unbroken bread of the letter.

((BEDA.)) The woman, a Gentile, but coming to the Lord with faith, signifies the Church gathered out of the Gentiles, who for her daughter, etc., *as far as* who leave the ancient dwellings of their perfidy, and betake themselves with pious devotion into the house of God, that is, the Church.

*Suffer first the children to be filled.* As if he said: It shall come to pass that you Gentiles also obtain salvation: but first the Jews, who by the ancient election are named the sons of God, must be refreshed with the heavenly bread, and so at last the food of life be ministered to the Gentiles. *Of the children. ((BEDA.))* A wondrous turning about: for Israel was once the son, we the dogs. According to the diversity of faith the order of the names is changed. Of them it is said: *Many dogs have compassed me ((Psal. XXI))*. Of us: *Other sheep I have, that are not of this fold ((Joan. X))*.

*Of the crumbs.* I am not worthy to receive whole meats; I am content with the leavings of the whelps, that so I may come to the whole bread. *((BEDA.)) Of the crumbs,* etc. The table is Scripture, whence: *Thou hast prepared a table before me,* etc. ((Psal. XXII)). The crumbs of the children, etc., *as far as* that by the merit of humility they may raise themselves up to hope for the things above, the rewards which have been promised by the Lord in heaven.

*For this saying. ((BEDA.))* Here is given an example of catechizing and baptizing infants, because by the faith and confession of their parents little ones are freed from the demon in baptism, who cannot yet of themselves have understanding, or do anything of good or of evil.

*Of Tyre. ((HIERON.))* Tyre, meaning straitness, signifies Judea, to which the Lord says: *The bed is straitened and the covering short: the one cannot cover both, so that he may betake himself to other nations ((Isai. XVIII))*. *Sidon. ((HIERON.))* Sidon, a hunting, an untamed wild beast, is our own region or nation. *Of Decapolis. ((BEDA.))* The region of ten cities beyond the Jordan toward the east. But where it is said: *He came to the sea of Galilee, through the midst of the coasts of Decapolis,* this does not signify that he entered them; for neither is he said to have sailed across the sea, but to have come as far as the sea, and to a place which looked toward the midst of the coasts of Decapolis, set far beyond the sea.

((HIERON.)) The Saviour is led by the apostles to the saving of the Gentiles, and teaches what he answered to the young man who questioned him: *Thou knowest the commandments; do these things, and thou shalt live ((Luc. XVIII))*.

*One deaf and dumb. ((BEDA.))* One, namely, who opens neither his ears to hear the words of God, nor his mouth to speak them. Such men they who have learned by long use to hear and to speak the word of God must needs offer to the Lord to be healed, that those whom human frailty cannot [heal], the right hand of grace may save.

((HIERON.)) The human race, as one man consumed by divers plagues in the first-formed man, is blinded while it sees, is made deaf while it hears, its nose is wiped while it smells, it is struck dumb while it speaks, it is made maimed while it lifts up its hands, it is bowed down while it is raised up, it becomes dropsical while it lusts, lame while it goes forward, it is overspread with leprosy while it is cleansed, it is filled with a demon while it aspires to divinity, it dies the death while it boldly excuses itself. *And they besought him.* The prophets and the patriarchs desired the incarnation of the Lord.

*And taking him,* etc. He who deserves to be healed is led apart from turbulent thoughts, from disordered deeds, and from ill-composed discourses. The fingers which are put into the ears are the words of the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said: *This is the finger of God ((Exod. VIII))*. And: *The heavens are the works of thy fingers ((Psal. VIII))*. *He touched his tongue,* etc. The foam from the flesh of the Lord is the divine wisdom, which looses the ignorance of the human race, so that it may say: I believe in God the Father almighty, etc. *Apart. ((BEDA.))* The first way of salvation is to be led out from the crowd. The Lord leads the sick man out from the crowd, when the mind, by sins, etc., *as far as* therefore, spitting, he touches the tongue of the dumb man that it may be able to speak, when by the touch of his loving-kindness he forms mouths long brutish to utter the words of wisdom.

*And looking up,* etc. *((HIERON.)) He groaned.* He taught us to groan, and to lift up to heaven the treasure of our heart, which is purified by compunction of heart from the frivolous gladness of the flesh, as it is said: *I roared with the groaning of my heart; Lord, all my desire is before thee,* etc. *And he said to him: Ephpheta, which is, Be thou opened. With the heart we believe unto justice ((Rom. X))*, etc. *And immediately they were opened,* etc. The ears are opened to hymns and canticles and psalms. The tongue is loosed, that it may utter forth a good word, which neither threats nor words can restrain or forbid. Whence Paul: *I am bound, but the word of God is not bound in me ((I Tim. II))*.

*And he spoke right. ((BEDA.))* He alone speaks rightly, whether by confessing the Lord or by preaching to others, whose hearing divine grace brings back, that he may be able to hearken and be obedient to the heavenly commandments. Whose tongue the Lord instructs to speak by the touch of wisdom, which he himself is. Such a one can say: *O Lord, thou wilt open my lips ((Psal. V))*, etc.

*And he charged them that they should tell no man.* He taught that we must glory not in mighty works, but in the cross and in humiliation. *But the more he charged them,* etc. A city set on a mountain and looked upon from every side cannot be hid ((Matth. XV)): humility always goes before glory.

*Be thou opened.* Properly, to the ears. For the ears were to be opened for hearing, and the tongue was to be loosed that it might be able to speak. Whence it follows: *Immediately they were opened,* etc.

hymns.title: Justice alone is the way of the Lord
God the sculptor of the mountains
Walk in the light of God's counsel
Give me, the faith which can remove
Who shall stand in God's holy place

echoes.text: “‘You shall do no injustice in judgment. You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favoritism to the great; but you shall judge your neighbor in righteousness.
echoes.note: James condemns showing partiality (prosopolempsia) in the assembly. Leviticus 19:15 is the foundational prohibition: 'you shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great, but in righteousness shall you judge your neighbor.' The verbal and thematic correspondence is strong, and the same chapter supplies the love-command James quotes in v.8.

echoes.text: You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be afraid of the face of man, for the judgment is God’s. The case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.”
echoes.note: Deuteronomy 1:17 enjoins judges to 'not be partial in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike.' James's scene of seating the rich well and the poor poorly enacts the very partiality this Mosaic charge to judges forbids. Volume and recurrence support the echo though no quotation is made.

echoes.text: You shall not pervert justice. You shall not show partiality. You shall not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise, and perverts the words of the righteous.
echoes.note: 'You shall not pervert justice; you shall not be partial' reinforces the impartiality motif standing behind James's rebuke of favoritism toward the rich. Part of the cluster of Deuteronomic impartiality texts; less verbally distinctive than Leviticus 19:15.

echoes.text: These also are sayings of the wise. To show partiality in judgment is not good.
echoes.note: 'It is not good to show partiality in judgment.' James's wisdom idiom and concern with favoritism in judging ('judges with evil thoughts,' v.4) resonates with this proverb. Conceptual echo within the impartiality tradition.

echoes.text: He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes, and inherit the throne of glory. For the pillars of the earth are Yahweh’s. He has set the world on them.
echoes.note: Hannah's song: God 'raises up the poor from the dust... to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor.' James 2:5 says God chose the poor to be heirs of the kingdom, reversing the world's status-seating. The seating/inheritance reversal aligns closely with James's argument.

echoes.text: He raises up the poor out of the dust. Lifts up the needy from the ash heap;
echoes.note: 'He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes.' James 2:5's election of the poor to royal inheritance draws on this reversal-of-status theme common to the Psalms of the anawim.

echoes.text: He who despises his neighbor sins, but blessed is he who has pity on the poor.
echoes.note: 'Whoever despises his neighbor is a sinner, but blessed is he who is generous to the poor.' James rebukes those who 'dishonored the poor man' (v.6). Faint wisdom-tradition echo of honoring rather than shaming the poor.

echoes.text: Don’t exploit the poor, because he is poor; and don’t crush the needy in court; for Yahweh will plead their case, and plunder the life of those who plunder them.
echoes.note: 'Do not rob the poor... for the LORD will plead their cause.' James 2:6 describes the rich who oppress and 'drag you before the courts.' Faint echo of the oppressed-poor / oppressor-rich topos; the Lord's vindication is implied in James's eschatology.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh: “For three transgressions of Israel, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment; because they have sold the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes; They trample on the dust of the earth on the head of the poor, and deny justice to the oppressed; and a man and his father use the same maiden, to profane my holy name;
echoes.note: Amos indicts those who 'sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals... trample the head of the poor.' James's portrait of rich oppressors dragging the poor to court stands in this prophetic stream of social critique. Conceptual, not verbal.

echoes.text: Hear this, you who desire to swallow up the needy, and cause the poor of the land to fail, Saying, ‘When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell grain? And the Sabbath, that we may market wheat, making the ephah small, and the shekel large, and dealing falsely with balances of deceit; that we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes, and sell the sweepings with the wheat?’”
echoes.note: Amos condemns those who 'trample on the needy and bring the poor of the land to an end.' James 2:6's oppressing rich participate in the same prophetic denunciation of economic exploitation. Faint thematic resonance.

echoes.text: The son of the Israelite woman blasphemed the Name, and cursed; and they brought him to Moses. His mother’s name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan.
echoes.note: The blasphemer who 'blasphemed the Name' (ha-Shem) in Leviticus 24 underlies Jewish reverence for the divine Name. James 2:7 says the rich 'blaspheme the honorable name by which you are called.' Faint allusion to the gravity of blaspheming the Name invoked over God's people.

echoes.text: that they may possess the remnant of Edom, and all the nations who are called by my name,” says Yahweh who does this.
echoes.note: '...all the nations who are called by my name' (cited at Acts 15:17 in the Jacobite context). James 2:7's 'honorable name by which you are called' evokes the biblical idiom of bearing God's name. Faint and contested as a direct source.

echoes.text: All the peoples of the earth shall see that you are called by Yahweh’s name, and they will be afraid of you.
echoes.note: 'All the peoples of the earth shall see that you are called by the name of the LORD.' James 2:7's language of bearing the honorable name draws on this covenantal idiom of God's name invoked over his people. Faint background echo.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: Explicit quotation introduced as 'the Scripture': 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' James names this the 'royal law.' This is a formal citation of Leviticus 19:18, the same Holiness Code chapter that grounds his impartiality argument.

echoes.text: “You shall not murder.
echoes.note: James cites 'Do not commit murder' as the word of the lawgiver (v.11). This is the Decalogue commandment, Exodus 20:13. Quoted alongside the adultery commandment to argue the law's unity.

echoes.text: “You shall not commit adultery.
echoes.note: James cites 'Do not commit adultery' (v.11) from the Decalogue, Exodus 20:14. The pairing of adultery and murder is a formal scriptural citation establishing that breaking one point makes one a transgressor of all.

echoes.text: “You shall not murder.
echoes.note: The Decalogue's murder prohibition also appears at Deuteronomy 5:17; James's citation draws on the Decalogue in either form. Listed as an alternate source for the murder commandment quoted in v.11.

echoes.text: “You shall not commit adultery.
echoes.note: The adultery prohibition also stands at Deuteronomy 5:18; James's quotation reflects the Decalogue. Provided as the Deuteronomic parallel to the Exodus citation in v.11.

echoes.text: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.
echoes.note: 'Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered.' James 2:13 says 'judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy.' The lex talionis of mercy/mercilessness is closely paralleled.

echoes.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: '...to do justice, and to love mercy (hesed), and to walk humbly with your God.' James's exaltation of mercy as triumphing over judgment (v.13) draws on the prophetic prizing of mercy as the heart of covenant obedience.

echoes.text: “Thus has Yahweh of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother. Don’t oppress the widow, nor the fatherless, the foreigner, nor the poor; and let none of you devise evil against his brother in your heart.’
echoes.note: 'Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy... do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor.' James links impartial judgment with mercy toward the poor in the same breath. Strong thematic correspondence.

echoes.text: He that takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord; And he will surely make firm his sins. Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray. Man cherisheth anger against man; And does he seek healing from the Lord? Upon a man like himself he has no mercy; And does he make supplication for his own sins?
echoes.note: Ben Sira: 'Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned... Does anyone harbor anger against another, and expect healing from the Lord?' James 2:13's principle that the merciless receive merciless judgment closely parallels this deuterocanonical wisdom on reciprocal mercy.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's almsgiving counsel: 'give alms from your possessions... almsgiving delivers from death.' James's coupling of mercy/almsgiving with deliverance at judgment (v.13) resonates with this deuterocanonical theology of merciful deeds. Conceptual echo.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.' Background to James's mercy-rewarded-at-judgment principle. Faint wisdom echo within the mercy cluster.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]
echoes.note: Jesus' withdrawal to the region of Tyre and Sidon and his healing of a Gentile woman's child recalls Elijah's sojourn with the Sidonian widow of Zarephath, whose son he restored, the paradigm of an Israelite prophet bringing life to a Gentile woman of that very coastland. Geographic and typological coherence is strong; the Sidonian-widow precedent frames the boundary-crossing mercy.

echoes.text: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”
echoes.note: The 'children first... then the dogs' logic enacts the order of salvation in which blessing comes to Israel first and through Israel to the nations ('in you all families of the earth shall be blessed'). The Syrophoenician's faith anticipates the Abrahamic extension of blessing beyond Israel. Figural and contested, but thematically coherent with election-then-overflow.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: The servant's mission to be 'a light to the nations' so that salvation reaches the ends of the earth resonates with the children's bread overflowing to a Gentile. Mark's narrative geography (Tyre, Decapolis) participates in the prophetic vision of the nations drawn in; faint figural availability.

echoes.text: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.
echoes.note: Jesus' priority 'let the children be filled first' presupposes Israel's status as God's chosen children/people set apart from the nations (Deuteronomy 7's election language). The exchange negotiates that elect-Israel-first economy; availability strong, verbal volume faint.

echoes.text: For dogs have surrounded me. A company of evildoers have enclosed me. They have pierced my hands and feet.
echoes.note: The 'dogs' metaphor for Gentiles draws on a stock OT pejorative (e.g., 'dogs have surrounded me'), here softened to household pups under the table. The idiom's OT background gives the insult-and-reversal its bite. Lexical availability; contested and faint.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: The healing of a deaf man with a speech impediment, climaxing in 'he makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak,' enacts Isaiah's eschatological promise: 'then the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped... and the tongue of the mute shall sing.' Mark signals the messianic age dawning; volume, recurrence (cf. Isa 29:18; 42:18), and thematic coherence are all high.

echoes.text: God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.
echoes.note: The crowd's acclamation 'he has done all things well' (panta kalos pepoieken) echoes the creation refrain that God saw all he had made and it was 'very good' (LXX kala lian), casting Jesus' restorative work as a new creation. The verbal contact (kalos / kala) and theme of God making/doing all things well give the allusion real volume.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness. The humble also will increase their joy in Yahweh, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.
echoes.note: 'In that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book, and the eyes of the blind shall see' reinforces the deaf-hearing motif of Isaiah 35 and ties back to the chapter's earlier Isaiah 29:13 citation, giving recurrence within the same prophetic source. The opening of ears is the visible sign of the promise.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to him, “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh?
echoes.note: 'Who makes a man mute, or deaf... Is it not I, the LORD?' grounds the claim that making the deaf hear and the mute speak is a divine prerogative. The crowd's wonder implicitly attributes to Jesus a work Yahweh claims as his own. Thematic coherence high; specific verbal volume moderate.

echoes.text: “Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see.
echoes.note: 'Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see' belongs to the cluster of Isaianic deaf/mute imagery animating this healing. A secondary witness reinforcing recurrence within Isaiah; fainter than 35:5-6.

echoes.text: Because wisdom opened the mouth of the dumb, And made the tongues of babes to speak clearly.
echoes.note: 'Wisdom opened the mouth of the mute, and made the tongues of infants speak clearly' (of the Exodus deliverance) is a Second-Temple text pairing divine wisdom with the loosing of mute tongues, resonant with Jesus loosing the tongue so the man 'spoke clearly.' Deuterocanonical availability; contested and faint.

echoes.text: For then I will purify the lips of the peoples, that they may all call on Yahweh’s name, to serve him shoulder to shoulder.
echoes.note: 'For then I will restore to the peoples a pure speech' offers an eschatological loosing-of-tongues motif consonant with the man speaking plainly in the Gentile Decapolis. Geographic-thematic resonance; very faint and contested.

doctrine.title: General Rules
doctrine.article: doing good to bodies and souls

notes.text: Your God — Tho' he seems to be departed, he will come to you, and abide with you. He will shortly come in the flesh, to execute vengeance upon the enemies of God.
Then — The poor Gentiles, who before were blind and deaf, shall now have the eyes and ears of their minds opened to see God's works, and to hear and receive his word.

Streams — The most dry and barren places shall be made moist and fruitful; which is principally meant of the plentiful effusion of God's grace upon such persons and nations, as had been wholly destitute of it. Rushes - Those dry and parched deserts, in which dragons have their abode, shall yield abundance of grass, and reeds, and rushes, which grow only in moist ground.

glossa.text: *The greenness of the reed.* The fulfilling of Scripture, which is signified by the reed; and the help of the intention, which by the rush: for the reed and the rush spring up and grow green beside the waters.

notes.text: That day — As soon as ever he is dead. Thoughts - All his designs and endeavours either for himself or for others.

For ever — Both because he liveth forever to fulfil his promises, and because he is eternally faithful. The psalmist praises God for his care over the church, ver. 1-14. His government over all, ver. 15-18. His giving his word to Israel, ver. 19, 20.

glossa.text: *Alleluia.* ((CAS.)) This voice, as it were saving musics *musicas*; read *musica*, "a saving music", like a heavenly harmony, which delights not men only but angels also, setting forth the praise of God. And it is fitly prefixed to this psalm, where the just man exhorts his soul to the praise of God: because in adversities the soul is sometimes troubled, whether it will or no. Whence above: *Why art thou sad, O my soul, and why dost thou disquiet me?* But that he may take away her disquiet, he suggests joy out of hope, if not out of the thing itself: *Hope in God,* etc. ((AUG.)) This soul, lifted up by hope, praises God here. ((CAS.)) First, he counsels himself, as it were all men, to praise, lest prayer be made among vain things; and as though acquiescing in the counsel, he affirms that he will praise there where he shall be able to praise fully. Secondly, he admonishes others not to hope in man, there: *Trust not.* Thirdly, he teaches that all hope is to be placed in the Almighty, there: *Blessed,* etc.

*Praise the Lord, O my soul.* But it is asked, by whom, and to whom, is this counsel given? If it be said that the flesh counsels the soul, this does not seem to be true, since counsel is wont to be given by the better and the worthier to the inferior: but the flesh is inferior to the soul. For the soul, although it be blamed because it is a sinner, is nevertheless called better by nature than the body that is praised in its own kind, because a spiritual nature excels the body, which it moves, rules, endows with sense, and apprehends: and being itself unbounded, it is near to the substance of God. So gold, blamed because it is foul, surpasses lead in purity, praise *laudatio*; read *laudato*, "that is praised": so too a bad man surpasses the best of horses. Counsel therefore is not given to the soul by the flesh, however greatly it be subdued and made peaceable: which nevertheless is dead because of sin. Nor yet does the mortal flesh counsel the immortal soul, because it is always beneath the soul; but the higher part of the soul, that is, the mind, which thinks upon the divine wisdom, cleaving to it and sighing after it, sees certain of its own parts troubled by the motions of the world, and hurried away to outward things by the desire of earthly goods: whence it calls it back to things inward and higher. Exhorting itself therefore according to its sensuality, it says: *Praise the Lord, O my soul.* For what pleases thee in this world? Divided among so many loves of the things of the ages, gather thyself to thy Author: here is peace and security for thee. Then the soul answers the mind, as one weighed down here and not able to leave off, as is meet. *I will praise in life.* Here in death I shall praise but thinly, because the body *is a load upon the soul, and the earthly habitation presseth down the sense that thinketh upon many things ((Sap. IX))*; here hope feeds us, life is in the world to come.

*In my life.* ((CAS.)) When I shall have cleaved to him perfectly, from whom to be parted, as now befalls, is death: but hope consoles, in which, living after a sort, it praises.

*As long as.* Not that at some time he shall not be, because he shall be for ever, and therefore truly long.

*Trust not,* etc. ((CAS.)) The second part. The counsel being given and confirmed, where he shall be able to praise fully, he admonishes them, as though set far off, and in the meantime while evils last (by which the soul is troubled), not to hope in man, but in God. ((AUG.)) Or, as one set in mind at the end of the world: he teaches them not to love things soon to end in place of things eternal; as if by my example also, *trust not,* etc. *In the children of men.* ((ID.)) In one son of man is salvation, and in him do ye hope. Not because he is a son of man, but because he is the Son of God. Not for that which he took from thee, but for that which he kept in himself.
*His spirit shall go forth,* etc. ((CAS.)) First he cleanses hearts by forbidding what is hurtful, that afterward he may aim at what is saving by admonishing to wholesome things.

*Blessed is he whose God is the God of Jacob.* ((CAS.)) The third part, where he teaches that the whole hope is to be placed in the Almighty, whom he describes from his works, that the Gentile world, so often confuted, may be still. ((AUG.)) Hurtful things being removed, he teaches what belongs to salvation, namely, in whom hope is to be placed. *His helper is his hope.* ((CAS.)) Of that Jacob himself he was so the helper, etc., *as far as* that is, of this true Jacob, as of that one.

*Who made heaven and earth.* ((ID.)) Because the worshippers of demons also have hope in their god, he determines in whom hope ought to be, that is, in Christ, and this he shows even to the end of the psalm, describing him through all things. *All things that are in them.* Lest thou think any other to be the creator, or that there exists a creator even of the smallest things.

*Who keepeth truth for ever.* ((CAS.)) Christ, who is the truth; every man is a liar. *He executeth judgment.* These two pertain to justice. Christ the judge avenges those who suffer for his name, and gives food to them that love him. *For them that suffer wrong.* ((AUG.)) Not every trouble is a wrong. What thou sufferest by right is not a wrong, as is that which the robber and other wicked men suffer. It is one thing therefore to suffer wrong, another to suffer punishment. For a man suffers punishment by right, but wrong is contrary to right.

*The Lord looseth them that are fettered.* ((CAS.)) This belongs to the abundance of his sweetness.

*The Lord lifteth up them that are cast down.* Whom the devil casts down, the Lord lifts up.

*He loveth the just.* ((CAS.)) Whom he sets in eternal blessedness.

*The fatherless and the widow he will receive.* *suseipiet* ((AUG.)) The whole Church of the Gentiles is come as a stranger to the fathers, a daughter not by flesh but by imitation.

*The fatherless* are all who are in pilgrimage, whose father is absent; and every faithful soul is a *widow* while the bridegroom is absent: whence they desire the more both the father and the bridegroom, and God protects them, not seen but desired.

*The Lord shall reign for ever.* ((CAS.)) This is of his magnificence.

He shall reign in us when our hearts shall be firm in him, which is not yet.

notes.text: My brethren -- the equality of Christians, intimated by this name, is the ground of the admonition. Hold not the faith of our common Lord, the Lord of glory — Of which glory all who believe in him partake. With respect of persons - That is, honour none merely for being rich; despise none merely for being poor.
With gold rings — Which were not then so common as now.
Ye look upon him — With respect.

Ye distinguish not — To which the most respect is due, to the poor or to the rich. But are become evil-reasoning Judges - You reason ill, and so judge wrong: for fine apparel is no proof of worth in him that wears it.

Hearken — As if he had said, Stay, consider, ye that judge thus. Does not the presumption lie rather in favour of the poor man? Hath not God chosen the poor - That is, are not they whom God hath chosen, generally speaking, poor in this world? who yet are rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom - Consequently, the most honourable of men: and those whom God so highly honours, ought not ye to honour likewise?
Do not the rich often oppress you — By open violence; often drag you - Under colour of law.
Do not they blaspheme that worthy name — Of God and of Christ. The apostle speaks chiefly of rich heathens: but are Christians, so called, a whit behind them?
If ye fulfil the royal law — The supreme law of the great King which is love; and that to every man, poor as well as rich, ye do well. Lev. xix, 18.
Being convicted — By that very law. Exod. xxiii, 3.
Whosoever keepeth the whole law, except in one point, he is guilty of all — Is as liable to condemnation as if he had offended in every point.

glossa.text: *Do not hold the faith in respect of persons. As if he should say:* The Lord does not invite the rich to the faith and despise the poor, but he chose the poor in this world, and endowed them with faith. The world casts out the poor man, courts the rich; the faith of Christ on the contrary teaches that all the glory of the rich is as the flower of the grass, while mercy toward the poor flowers unto eternity. *Of the Lord of glory.* He names him the Lord of glory, that his commands may be obeyed, who repays with everlasting glory that which is given to the poor for love of him.

*Hearken. ((BED.))* Attend more diligently, because not those who are richer in the world, etc., *as far as* yet these he has rendered illustrious and noble by the expectation of the kingdom to come.

*Hath not God. ((BED.))* God chose the poor, who elsewhere says: *Fear not, little flock, for it hath pleased your Father to give you a kingdom.* He chose poor parents also, by whose office he himself should be nourished.

*Do not the rich.* More openly he shows whom he had called rich above, namely those who prefer riches to Christ, and, themselves strangers to the faith, oppress by power those who believe, and drag them to the judgment-seats of the more powerful. And there is another cause why they are not to be chosen, because they bring evils upon the faithful.
*They blaspheme.* In the times of the apostles many of the Gentiles and of the Jews, and especially the richer, are found to have done these things.

*If yet the law.* Because he had spoken harshly and concerning contempt of the rich, and in a manner contrary to the divine law, which commands that all be loved, lest the rich be thought to be despised altogether, he adds: as if he should say, for the aforesaid causes they are not to be chosen, but if you fulfil this law which says: *Thou shalt love thy neighbour ((Matth. XXII))*, you do well; because, although the rich are not to be chosen on account of their riches, yet they are not the less to be loved for God's sake.

*Royal.* That is, excellent, or because it is common to all, and embraces all. Or that which says: *Thou shalt not confound the person of the poor, nor honour the countenance of the mighty ((Levit. XIX))* , and elsewhere: *There shall be no difference of persons: you shall hear the little as the great, because it is the judgment of God ((Deut. I))*.

*But whosoever.* Lest they should think it a contemptible sin to transgress the law in this one matter, he adds: *But whosoever,* etc. *But offend in one, he is become guilty of all.* Truly he who offends in one point is a transgressor of the whole law, because he who sins acts against the author of the law, whom he slights in his own law, and against charity, which is the cause and mother of the whole law. Let us see this sentence from a like case: If anyone should offend me, he would offend all my brothers and friends in me, and in a manner would sin against all. So he who neglects one commandment renders useless to himself the rest, which, when fulfilled, seemed to help.

notes.text: Matt. xv, 21.
The woman was a Greek (that is, a Gentile, not a Jew) a Syrophenician or Canaanite. Canaan was also called Syrophenicia, as lying between Syria, properly so called, and Phenicia.
Matt. xv, 29.

He put his fingers into his ears — Perhaps intending to teach us, that we are not to prescribe to him (as they who brought this man attempted to do) but to expect his blessing by whatsoever means he pleases: even though there should be no proportion or resemblance between the means used, and the benefit to be conveyed thereby.

Ephphatha — This was a word of SOVEREIGN AUTHORITY, not an address to God for power to heal: such an address was needless; for Christ had a perpetual fund of power residing in himself, to work all miracles whenever he pleased, even to the raising the dead, John v, 21, 26.
Them — The blind man and those that brought him.

glossa.text: *And rising up from thence.* Leaving the Scribes and Pharisees, those calumniators, he withdrew into the parts of Tyre and Sidon, that he might heal the Tyrians and the Sidonians. *No man.* ((BEDA.)) Although he could not be hid, yet what he willed was not done. But an example, etc., *as far as* that he might free the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman from the demon, and by the faith of a Gentile woman convict the perfidy of the Scribes and the Pharisees.

*For a woman.* Mark says that the Lord was in the house when the woman came to him. Matthew says that *she crieth after us ((Matth. XV))*. By which he hints that she poured out her prayers behind him as he walked. The woman therefore came to him into the house, but because Matthew says: *He answered her not a word,* he gave it to be understood that both were silent, and that they entered in silence. And so the rest is woven together, and in nothing do they disagree.

((HIER.)) The woman is our Roman mother of the Church. The daughter is the demon-possessed barbarism of the West, whose faith made a sheep out of a dog. She seeks the crumbs of understanding; she does not desire the unbroken bread of the letter.

((BEDA.)) The woman, a Gentile, but coming to the Lord with faith, signifies the Church gathered out of the Gentiles, who for her daughter, etc., *as far as* who leave the ancient dwellings of their perfidy, and betake themselves with pious devotion into the house of God, that is, the Church.

*Suffer first the children to be filled.* As if he said: It shall come to pass that you Gentiles also obtain salvation: but first the Jews, who by the ancient election are named the sons of God, must be refreshed with the heavenly bread, and so at last the food of life be ministered to the Gentiles. *Of the children. ((BEDA.))* A wondrous turning about: for Israel was once the son, we the dogs. According to the diversity of faith the order of the names is changed. Of them it is said: *Many dogs have compassed me ((Psal. XXI))*. Of us: *Other sheep I have, that are not of this fold ((Joan. X))*.

*Of the crumbs.* I am not worthy to receive whole meats; I am content with the leavings of the whelps, that so I may come to the whole bread. *((BEDA.)) Of the crumbs,* etc. The table is Scripture, whence: *Thou hast prepared a table before me,* etc. ((Psal. XXII)). The crumbs of the children, etc., *as far as* that by the merit of humility they may raise themselves up to hope for the things above, the rewards which have been promised by the Lord in heaven.

*For this saying. ((BEDA.))* Here is given an example of catechizing and baptizing infants, because by the faith and confession of their parents little ones are freed from the demon in baptism, who cannot yet of themselves have understanding, or do anything of good or of evil.

*Of Tyre. ((HIERON.))* Tyre, meaning straitness, signifies Judea, to which the Lord says: *The bed is straitened and the covering short: the one cannot cover both, so that he may betake himself to other nations ((Isai. XVIII))*. *Sidon. ((HIERON.))* Sidon, a hunting, an untamed wild beast, is our own region or nation. *Of Decapolis. ((BEDA.))* The region of ten cities beyond the Jordan toward the east. But where it is said: *He came to the sea of Galilee, through the midst of the coasts of Decapolis,* this does not signify that he entered them; for neither is he said to have sailed across the sea, but to have come as far as the sea, and to a place which looked toward the midst of the coasts of Decapolis, set far beyond the sea.

((HIERON.)) The Saviour is led by the apostles to the saving of the Gentiles, and teaches what he answered to the young man who questioned him: *Thou knowest the commandments; do these things, and thou shalt live ((Luc. XVIII))*.

*One deaf and dumb. ((BEDA.))* One, namely, who opens neither his ears to hear the words of God, nor his mouth to speak them. Such men they who have learned by long use to hear and to speak the word of God must needs offer to the Lord to be healed, that those whom human frailty cannot [heal], the right hand of grace may save.

((HIERON.)) The human race, as one man consumed by divers plagues in the first-formed man, is blinded while it sees, is made deaf while it hears, its nose is wiped while it smells, it is struck dumb while it speaks, it is made maimed while it lifts up its hands, it is bowed down while it is raised up, it becomes dropsical while it lusts, lame while it goes forward, it is overspread with leprosy while it is cleansed, it is filled with a demon while it aspires to divinity, it dies the death while it boldly excuses itself. *And they besought him.* The prophets and the patriarchs desired the incarnation of the Lord.

*And taking him,* etc. He who deserves to be healed is led apart from turbulent thoughts, from disordered deeds, and from ill-composed discourses. The fingers which are put into the ears are the words of the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said: *This is the finger of God ((Exod. VIII))*. And: *The heavens are the works of thy fingers ((Psal. VIII))*. *He touched his tongue,* etc. The foam from the flesh of the Lord is the divine wisdom, which looses the ignorance of the human race, so that it may say: I believe in God the Father almighty, etc. *Apart. ((BEDA.))* The first way of salvation is to be led out from the crowd. The Lord leads the sick man out from the crowd, when the mind, by sins, etc., *as far as* therefore, spitting, he touches the tongue of the dumb man that it may be able to speak, when by the touch of his loving-kindness he forms mouths long brutish to utter the words of wisdom.

*And looking up,* etc. *((HIERON.)) He groaned.* He taught us to groan, and to lift up to heaven the treasure of our heart, which is purified by compunction of heart from the frivolous gladness of the flesh, as it is said: *I roared with the groaning of my heart; Lord, all my desire is before thee,* etc. *And he said to him: Ephpheta, which is, Be thou opened. With the heart we believe unto justice ((Rom. X))*, etc. *And immediately they were opened,* etc. The ears are opened to hymns and canticles and psalms. The tongue is loosed, that it may utter forth a good word, which neither threats nor words can restrain or forbid. Whence Paul: *I am bound, but the word of God is not bound in me ((I Tim. II))*.

*And he spoke right. ((BEDA.))* He alone speaks rightly, whether by confessing the Lord or by preaching to others, whose hearing divine grace brings back, that he may be able to hearken and be obedient to the heavenly commandments. Whose tongue the Lord instructs to speak by the touch of wisdom, which he himself is. Such a one can say: *O Lord, thou wilt open my lips ((Psal. V))*, etc.

*And he charged them that they should tell no man.* He taught that we must glory not in mighty works, but in the cross and in humiliation. *But the more he charged them,* etc. A city set on a mountain and looked upon from every side cannot be hid ((Matth. XV)): humility always goes before glory.

*Be thou opened.* Properly, to the ears. For the ears were to be opened for hearing, and the tongue was to be loosed that it might be able to speak. Whence it follows: *Immediately they were opened,* etc.

Prepare the way of the Lord
Wild and lone the prophet's voice
You who are thirsty, come to the well
Let my people seek their freedom
Lead on, O cloud of Presence

echoes.text: “‘You shall do no injustice in judgment. You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favoritism to the great; but you shall judge your neighbor in righteousness.
echoes.note: James condemns showing partiality (prosopolempsia) in the assembly. Leviticus 19:15 is the foundational prohibition: 'you shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great, but in righteousness shall you judge your neighbor.' The verbal and thematic correspondence is strong, and the same chapter supplies the love-command James quotes in v.8.

echoes.text: You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be afraid of the face of man, for the judgment is God’s. The case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me, and I will hear it.”
echoes.note: Deuteronomy 1:17 enjoins judges to 'not be partial in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike.' James's scene of seating the rich well and the poor poorly enacts the very partiality this Mosaic charge to judges forbids. Volume and recurrence support the echo though no quotation is made.

echoes.text: You shall not pervert justice. You shall not show partiality. You shall not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise, and perverts the words of the righteous.
echoes.note: 'You shall not pervert justice; you shall not be partial' reinforces the impartiality motif standing behind James's rebuke of favoritism toward the rich. Part of the cluster of Deuteronomic impartiality texts; less verbally distinctive than Leviticus 19:15.

echoes.text: These also are sayings of the wise. To show partiality in judgment is not good.
echoes.note: 'It is not good to show partiality in judgment.' James's wisdom idiom and concern with favoritism in judging ('judges with evil thoughts,' v.4) resonates with this proverb. Conceptual echo within the impartiality tradition.

echoes.text: He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes, and inherit the throne of glory. For the pillars of the earth are Yahweh’s. He has set the world on them.
echoes.note: Hannah's song: God 'raises up the poor from the dust... to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor.' James 2:5 says God chose the poor to be heirs of the kingdom, reversing the world's status-seating. The seating/inheritance reversal aligns closely with James's argument.

echoes.text: He raises up the poor out of the dust. Lifts up the needy from the ash heap;
echoes.note: 'He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes.' James 2:5's election of the poor to royal inheritance draws on this reversal-of-status theme common to the Psalms of the anawim.

echoes.text: He who despises his neighbor sins, but blessed is he who has pity on the poor.
echoes.note: 'Whoever despises his neighbor is a sinner, but blessed is he who is generous to the poor.' James rebukes those who 'dishonored the poor man' (v.6). Faint wisdom-tradition echo of honoring rather than shaming the poor.

echoes.text: Don’t exploit the poor, because he is poor; and don’t crush the needy in court; for Yahweh will plead their case, and plunder the life of those who plunder them.
echoes.note: 'Do not rob the poor... for the LORD will plead their cause.' James 2:6 describes the rich who oppress and 'drag you before the courts.' Faint echo of the oppressed-poor / oppressor-rich topos; the Lord's vindication is implied in James's eschatology.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh: “For three transgressions of Israel, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment; because they have sold the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes; They trample on the dust of the earth on the head of the poor, and deny justice to the oppressed; and a man and his father use the same maiden, to profane my holy name;
echoes.note: Amos indicts those who 'sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals... trample the head of the poor.' James's portrait of rich oppressors dragging the poor to court stands in this prophetic stream of social critique. Conceptual, not verbal.

echoes.text: Hear this, you who desire to swallow up the needy, and cause the poor of the land to fail, Saying, ‘When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell grain? And the Sabbath, that we may market wheat, making the ephah small, and the shekel large, and dealing falsely with balances of deceit; that we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes, and sell the sweepings with the wheat?’”
echoes.note: Amos condemns those who 'trample on the needy and bring the poor of the land to an end.' James 2:6's oppressing rich participate in the same prophetic denunciation of economic exploitation. Faint thematic resonance.

echoes.text: The son of the Israelite woman blasphemed the Name, and cursed; and they brought him to Moses. His mother’s name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan.
echoes.note: The blasphemer who 'blasphemed the Name' (ha-Shem) in Leviticus 24 underlies Jewish reverence for the divine Name. James 2:7 says the rich 'blaspheme the honorable name by which you are called.' Faint allusion to the gravity of blaspheming the Name invoked over God's people.

echoes.text: that they may possess the remnant of Edom, and all the nations who are called by my name,” says Yahweh who does this.
echoes.note: '...all the nations who are called by my name' (cited at Acts 15:17 in the Jacobite context). James 2:7's 'honorable name by which you are called' evokes the biblical idiom of bearing God's name. Faint and contested as a direct source.

echoes.text: All the peoples of the earth shall see that you are called by Yahweh’s name, and they will be afraid of you.
echoes.note: 'All the peoples of the earth shall see that you are called by the name of the LORD.' James 2:7's language of bearing the honorable name draws on this covenantal idiom of God's name invoked over his people. Faint background echo.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: Explicit quotation introduced as 'the Scripture': 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' James names this the 'royal law.' This is a formal citation of Leviticus 19:18, the same Holiness Code chapter that grounds his impartiality argument.

echoes.text: “You shall not murder.
echoes.note: James cites 'Do not commit murder' as the word of the lawgiver (v.11). This is the Decalogue commandment, Exodus 20:13. Quoted alongside the adultery commandment to argue the law's unity.

echoes.text: “You shall not commit adultery.
echoes.note: James cites 'Do not commit adultery' (v.11) from the Decalogue, Exodus 20:14. The pairing of adultery and murder is a formal scriptural citation establishing that breaking one point makes one a transgressor of all.

echoes.text: “You shall not murder.
echoes.note: The Decalogue's murder prohibition also appears at Deuteronomy 5:17; James's citation draws on the Decalogue in either form. Listed as an alternate source for the murder commandment quoted in v.11.

echoes.text: “You shall not commit adultery.
echoes.note: The adultery prohibition also stands at Deuteronomy 5:18; James's quotation reflects the Decalogue. Provided as the Deuteronomic parallel to the Exodus citation in v.11.

echoes.text: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.
echoes.note: 'Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered.' James 2:13 says 'judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy.' The lex talionis of mercy/mercilessness is closely paralleled.

echoes.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: '...to do justice, and to love mercy (hesed), and to walk humbly with your God.' James's exaltation of mercy as triumphing over judgment (v.13) draws on the prophetic prizing of mercy as the heart of covenant obedience.

echoes.text: “Thus has Yahweh of Armies spoken, saying, ‘Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother. Don’t oppress the widow, nor the fatherless, the foreigner, nor the poor; and let none of you devise evil against his brother in your heart.’
echoes.note: 'Render true judgments, show kindness and mercy... do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the sojourner, or the poor.' James links impartial judgment with mercy toward the poor in the same breath. Strong thematic correspondence.

echoes.text: He that takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord; And he will surely make firm his sins. Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray. Man cherisheth anger against man; And does he seek healing from the Lord? Upon a man like himself he has no mercy; And does he make supplication for his own sins?
echoes.note: Ben Sira: 'Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned... Does anyone harbor anger against another, and expect healing from the Lord?' James 2:13's principle that the merciless receive merciless judgment closely parallels this deuterocanonical wisdom on reciprocal mercy.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's almsgiving counsel: 'give alms from your possessions... almsgiving delivers from death.' James's coupling of mercy/almsgiving with deliverance at judgment (v.13) resonates with this deuterocanonical theology of merciful deeds. Conceptual echo.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.' Background to James's mercy-rewarded-at-judgment principle. Faint wisdom echo within the mercy cluster.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]
echoes.note: Jesus' withdrawal to the region of Tyre and Sidon and his healing of a Gentile woman's child recalls Elijah's sojourn with the Sidonian widow of Zarephath, whose son he restored, the paradigm of an Israelite prophet bringing life to a Gentile woman of that very coastland. Geographic and typological coherence is strong; the Sidonian-widow precedent frames the boundary-crossing mercy.

echoes.text: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”
echoes.note: The 'children first... then the dogs' logic enacts the order of salvation in which blessing comes to Israel first and through Israel to the nations ('in you all families of the earth shall be blessed'). The Syrophoenician's faith anticipates the Abrahamic extension of blessing beyond Israel. Figural and contested, but thematically coherent with election-then-overflow.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: The servant's mission to be 'a light to the nations' so that salvation reaches the ends of the earth resonates with the children's bread overflowing to a Gentile. Mark's narrative geography (Tyre, Decapolis) participates in the prophetic vision of the nations drawn in; faint figural availability.

echoes.text: For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. Yahweh your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.
echoes.note: Jesus' priority 'let the children be filled first' presupposes Israel's status as God's chosen children/people set apart from the nations (Deuteronomy 7's election language). The exchange negotiates that elect-Israel-first economy; availability strong, verbal volume faint.

echoes.text: For dogs have surrounded me. A company of evildoers have enclosed me. They have pierced my hands and feet.
echoes.note: The 'dogs' metaphor for Gentiles draws on a stock OT pejorative (e.g., 'dogs have surrounded me'), here softened to household pups under the table. The idiom's OT background gives the insult-and-reversal its bite. Lexical availability; contested and faint.

echoes.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing; for waters will break out in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
echoes.note: The healing of a deaf man with a speech impediment, climaxing in 'he makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak,' enacts Isaiah's eschatological promise: 'then the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped... and the tongue of the mute shall sing.' Mark signals the messianic age dawning; volume, recurrence (cf. Isa 29:18; 42:18), and thematic coherence are all high.

echoes.text: God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.
echoes.note: The crowd's acclamation 'he has done all things well' (panta kalos pepoieken) echoes the creation refrain that God saw all he had made and it was 'very good' (LXX kala lian), casting Jesus' restorative work as a new creation. The verbal contact (kalos / kala) and theme of God making/doing all things well give the allusion real volume.

echoes.text: In that day, the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness. The humble also will increase their joy in Yahweh, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.
echoes.note: 'In that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book, and the eyes of the blind shall see' reinforces the deaf-hearing motif of Isaiah 35 and ties back to the chapter's earlier Isaiah 29:13 citation, giving recurrence within the same prophetic source. The opening of ears is the visible sign of the promise.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to him, “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh?
echoes.note: 'Who makes a man mute, or deaf... Is it not I, the LORD?' grounds the claim that making the deaf hear and the mute speak is a divine prerogative. The crowd's wonder implicitly attributes to Jesus a work Yahweh claims as his own. Thematic coherence high; specific verbal volume moderate.

echoes.text: “Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see.
echoes.note: 'Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see' belongs to the cluster of Isaianic deaf/mute imagery animating this healing. A secondary witness reinforcing recurrence within Isaiah; fainter than 35:5-6.

echoes.text: Because wisdom opened the mouth of the dumb, And made the tongues of babes to speak clearly.
echoes.note: 'Wisdom opened the mouth of the mute, and made the tongues of infants speak clearly' (of the Exodus deliverance) is a Second-Temple text pairing divine wisdom with the loosing of mute tongues, resonant with Jesus loosing the tongue so the man 'spoke clearly.' Deuterocanonical availability; contested and faint.

echoes.text: For then I will purify the lips of the peoples, that they may all call on Yahweh’s name, to serve him shoulder to shoulder.
echoes.note: 'For then I will restore to the peoples a pure speech' offers an eschatological loosing-of-tongues motif consonant with the man speaking plainly in the Gentile Decapolis. Geographic-thematic resonance; very faint and contested.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The rich and the poor have this in common:
the Lord is the maker of them all.
Even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs.
And the door we shut, Christ throws open wide.
He touched the deaf man's ears and said: Ephphatha.
Be opened, and his ears were opened.
Open our ears, our hands, our doors; come, let us worship.
Be opened, O Lord. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: A foreign woman kneels and will not be turned away; even the dogs, she says, eat the crumbs under the table, and her faith pries the door open.
Be opened.
They bring him a man who cannot hear or speak; he takes him aside, touches his ears and his tongue, looks up to heaven, and sighs: Ephphatha.
Be opened.
The rich and the poor meet together, and the Lord is the maker of them all; show no partiality, for God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith.
Be opened.
So unstop our ears to the ones we have not heard, open our hands to the ones we have passed by, and fling these doors wide.
Be opened, O Lord, and let us in.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Even the dogs eat the crumbs beneath the table.
Be opened.
He touched his ears and said: Ephphatha.
Be opened.
The Lord is the maker of rich and poor alike.
Be opened.
Open our ears and hands; come, let us worship.
Be opened, O Lord. Amen.
